section_1.title: Review: The Geometric Foundation
section_1.content: Briefly recap vectors in R² (arrows starting at origin). Define a vector as an object that follows two rules: Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication. Visualize these as stretching and shifting arrows on a grid.
section_1.example: An arrow representing a force acting on a bird, where doubling the scalar doubles the force magnitude.

section_2.title: The Leap to Abstraction
section_2.content: Introduce the idea that 'vectors' don't have to be arrows. They can be functions, matrices, or polynomials. As long as they satisfy the '8 Axioms of Vector Spaces', they are vectors. Think of the Vector Space as a 'container' that obeys specific algebraic laws.
section_2.example: Representing a sound wave (function) as a vector; adding two sound waves produces a new sound wave, keeping it within the 'space' of all sounds.

section_3.title: Testing the Rules: The Axiom Checklist
section_3.content: Display a graphical checklist of the 8 axioms (Closure, Commutativity, Associativity, Identity, Inverse, Distributivity). Use a toggle switch animation: If the set passes all, it's a Vector Space; if it breaks even one, it's rejected.
section_3.example: A robotic arm's movement constraints; if the 'set of reachable positions' doesn't contain the zero-point (starting position), it fails the vector space test.

section_4.title: Visualizing Abstract Spaces
section_4.content: Use a 3D animation morphing an arrow into a polynomial curve. Show that the underlying 'logic' of the operations remains identical despite the change in physical appearance. This reinforces that abstract spaces are just generalized versions of our 2D grid.
section_4.example: An animator manipulating a character's facial expression using a set of 'basis' expressions (blending shapes) which act exactly like vector components.

section_5.title: Conclusion & Takeaway
section_5.content: Summarize that abstract vector spaces provide a universal language for complex systems. Whether dealing with quantum states or data science, the rules of linear algebra provide the structure.
section_5.example: A data scientist categorizing animal species by features; treating each feature set as a vector in an 'N-dimensional biological space'.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.2 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
